hook_text: Most learners walk to school. True or not, that sentence earns zero marks in a data report. Three words fix it.
clip_script: You surveyed sixty Grade 9 learners and you write: most learners walk to school. Zero marks. Why? Because a claim without a number is just an opinion. Fix it with three parts. Claim: walking is the most common way to school. Number: 33 of 60, which is 55 percent. Caution: this is a sample from Grade 9, so other grades might differ. Claim, number, caution. Again. Claim: girls use taxis more than boys. Number: 12 of 30 girls, 40 percent, against 9 of 30 boys, 30 percent. Caution: that is three learners in thirty, so another sample could shrink the gap. Now predict for the whole grade of 300: about 55 percent, so ABOUT 165 walkers. Not 165. About 165. The weather service never says it will rain; it says 70 percent chance. Your report follows the same rule. Every finding: claim, number, caution. Say it with me.
visual_style: The bare sentence most learners walk appears and gets a red zero; three boxes labelled claim, number, caution slide in and fill with text; a two-way table glows where each number comes from; the word about pulses in front of 165.
pacing: Zero marks fast, the three-part build at speaking pace, the second example quicker, the forecast rule slow.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for the eight parts of a report, handling outliers honestly and writing limitations with their directions.
